item.title: IDEA: Can you save money with a theme park annual pass? We did the math
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Annual passes to major U.S. theme parks like Walt Disney World, Universal Orlando Resort, SeaWorld and Legoland come with a long list of benefits. You can visit as often as you like; you get discounts on extras like parking, merchandise and dining; and your pass often comes with access to special events throughout the year. Theme park annual passes also come with a hefty price tag that can climb upward of $1,000. Because of this, it can be easy to assume an annual pass is only worth the cost if you live near one of these parks and can visit every week. As an out-of-state resident who has held an annual pass to Universal Orlando Resort since 2020, I can assure you that assumption is incorrect. But you don't have to take my word for it. I calculated the break-even point for 10 theme parks across the country to help you decide whether it's an option worth looking into. For consistency, I based these calculations on each park's top-tier pass and the lowest one-day ticket prices, using park-to-park tickets at resorts with multiple parks, since annual passes include park-to-park access. Because these calculations are based on one-day tickets, you would still need to determine whether you could save money with an annual pass by considering the ticket cost on the date(s) of your visit (most parks have variable pricing), how many trips you take each year and the number of days you visit per trip. **About 6 once you factor in the cost of free parking and the Express passes Disney World offers several annual passes, but only one, the Disney Incredi-Pass, is available to out-of-state residents. The Disney Incredi-Pass has no blockout dates and includes complimentary theme park parking. If you were to visit only on the cheapest days of the year, you would need to visit nine times each year to realize the value of a Disney World annual pass as a non-Florida resident. When you factor in shopping and dining discounts and free parking, you can probably break even after eight visits. But if you were to visit on the more expensive days, you could break even in closer to six days. Remember, though, this comparison is based on the one-day ticket price. If you plan to spend eight days at Disney World broken up between one or two visits per year, you could potentially do better to buy a multiday park hopper ticket versus an annual pass. Because Disney uses variable ticket pricing and tickets get less expensive as you add more days, you have to do the math to find out which is best for you. Don't worry, the math on most other parks isn't quite as involved. Disneyland's top-tier pass is called the Inspire Key. At $1,899 per year, this pass has blackout dates during the weeks of Christmas and New Year's Eve, and it includes free standard parking and unlimited Disney PhotoPass downloads. The Inspire Key pass can pay for itself after 11 visits, since the lowest park hopper tickets start at $179. As with Disney World, the number of visits required to break even would decrease if you visited on more expensive days, and you could still save money by purchasing multiday tickets. Universal Orlando has several annual pass options, but the 2-Park Premier Pass is the easiest to use and has the most benefits. You get park-to-park admission between Universal Studios Florida and Universal Islands of Adventure, complimentary skip-the-line Express passes after 4 p.m., complimentary valet and prime parking, one free ticket to Halloween Horror Nights, early park admission and several valuable discounts. If you were to visit during the holidays when one-day park-to-park tickets climb as high as $255, you can break even after four days. It's also worth doing the calculations with the included Halloween Horror Nights ticket, which starts at $99. When you factor that in, you can break even after five visits. A six-day park-to-park ticket that also includes access to Universal Epic Universe is only $550.99 per person, so if you only plan to visit once per year for six days, you would save significantly by purchasing a multiday ticket versus an annual pass. Universal Studios Hollywood only has one park, making the math here easier to calculate. The park's Platinum Annual Pass has no blockout dates and includes free general parking most of the year, one Halloween Horror Nights ticket and Express skip-the-line access after 3 p.m. You'd technically have to visit 6.0025 times to break even, but if you include the free parking and after-3 p.m. Express passes, we can safely say you break even after six visits. Similar to Universal Orlando, you can break even sooner if you factor in the cost of a Halloween Horror Nights ticket, which starts at $77 per person. When you factor that in, plus those other perks, you can break even after approximately five one-day visits. This is where things get a little bit fun (in my opinion, anyway). Legoland's Premium Annual Pass includes visits to more than 20 Merlin attractions across the country, including Legoland, Peppa Pig Park, Sea Life Aquarium, Madame Tussauds wax museum and more. A lot of these parks are in theme park hubs like Florida, California and Texas, so you likely aren't too far from one or multiple locations. In this case, you don't need to plan multiple visits to a single park to see the value in an annual pass. You can visit multiple locations around the country with no blockout dates, free parking and four free "Bring-a-Friend" tickets (one ticket per quarter), which make the math very appealing. If you assign a $69 value to the "Bring-A-Friend" tickets, four per year would equal $276, just $23 less than the total annual pass cost. So, if you were to visit one of the 20+ parks nationwide four times per year (once per quarter) and bring a friend or family member with you, you'd save money with an annual pass before even factoring in free parking and other discounts. This is another instance where you can access multiple parks with a single annual pass. SeaWorld Orlando's Platinum Pass includes unlimited admission to 11 parks across the country with no blockout dates. These include all SeaWorld and Busch Gardens parks, as well as their affiliated water parks. You also get eight free guest tickets, free photos and free preferred parking. A few notes here. You can't use all eight free guest tickets at the same time and they are limited to select parks. SeaWorld allows you to use a certain number of tickets during different calendar windows throughout the year. But if you were to visit these parks eight times per year and bring a friend, you would save more than $600 by purchasing an annual pass. It's also worth noting that SeaWorld San Diego's Platinum Pass is only $201 on sale, and its lowest one-day ticket costs $64.99, so you'd break even after just four visits. While it provides the passholder access to the same 11 parks, its guest passes can only be used at the California parks. Opened in July 2026, Universal Kids Resort is the newest park on this list. The park recently started selling annual passes, with the Gold Annual Pass being its top-tier offering. The Gold pass has no blockout dates and includes regular self-parking. Assuming you visit on five separate days and only visit on the least expensive days, you would break even after five visits. But because the Gold Pass also includes free parking and other discounts, you could potentially break even in four one-day visits. Because the park also sells discounted multiday tickets, the above math only makes sense if you were to visit on five nonconsecutive days. You don't need to live in Florida or California to have access to award-winning theme parks. Holiday World in Santa Claus, Indiana, consistently wins awards for its cleanliness, water park and thrilling coasters. Holiday World's Platinum Pass has no blockout dates, early entry for select attractions and discounted "Bring-a-Friend" tickets. Holiday World already offers free parking, sunscreen and soft drinks, so you won't get additional discounts there. You would break even after four one-day visits, assuming you purchase the lowest-cost tickets. Dollywood's top-of-the-line pass is a Diamond Season Pass (a very fitting name for our bright and shining queen Dolly Parton, if you ask me). With it, you get unlimited visits, complimentary parking, Time Saver skip-the-line access for the first hour of each day, a 20% discount on shopping and dining, and four free "Bring-a-Friend" tickets. Dollywood handles its "Bring-a-Friend" tickets differently. You can use them one at a time or all four at once. If you brought four friends with you during your first visit after buying your annual pass, you would have more than covered the cost of your pass. In fact, you could save about $110 by purchasing an annual pass instead of five one-day tickets (you and four friends). Any future visits that year are just a bonus. Just one of the million reasons to love Dollywood. Silver Dollar City and Dollywood are owned by the same parent company (Herschend Family Entertainment), but their annual passes work quite differently. Silver Dollar City's Diamond Pass includes unlimited visits to the park and White Water water park, eight free "Bring A Friend" tickets (to be used during specific redemption windows at Silver Dollar City or White Water), a bonus "Bring-a-Friend" ticket you can use on any day and $29.99 tickets for friends and family. Even though you can't use all of your "Bring-a-Friend" tickets at one time, you only need to visit with a guest twice to break even with an annual pass before even digging into the savings you would find from in-park discounts. In addition to the advertised benefits, there is a level of convenience that comes with being a passholder. You can pop in for a few hours without feeling like you wasted money on a full-day ticket, and you feel like a more valuable guest when you visit. I often get things like priority parade seating, fun freebies and passholder-only discounts of up to 70% off merchandise. No amount of math matters unless you know you will actually use and enjoy the benefits of being a passholder. Use these calculations as a jumping-off point to decide if you are ready to be a passholder.

item.title: Why is there so much kissing in Spain?
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
Why is there so much kissing in Spain? In Spain, kissing in public is an everyday sight. But the country's comfort with public affection reveals a surprising history of repression and rebellion. Kissing is everywhere in Spain. There's the double-cheek kiss when you meet someone, of course. But then there are the romantic ones. I've been stuck behind a middle-aged couple who stop to smooch on a busy high street. I've felt a pang of nostalgia seeing teens kissing in sun-soaked parks and I've squeezed past tipsy revellers canoodling while fireworks crackle at Valencia's Las Fallas festival. Even my accountant signs off her emails with "besos" (kisses). After more than six years living in Spain, I've become used to these public displays of affection. But when a friend returned to Valencia after a trip to Japan, she noticed them immediately. Stepping out of the train station, she was greeted by a couple snogging on a bench. After her stint in a country where PDA is far less frequent, the sight filled her with relief. "I'm home," she thought. It made me wonder: is Spain really a country of kissing? And what can these public displays of affection tell us about its culture, history and attitudes towards intimacy? One explanation may lie in the way Spaniards use public spaces. In many parts of the country, everyday life takes place outdoors, in busy streets, cafes and parks. A University of Warwick study found that Spain was among the countries that required the least personal space when meeting a new acquaintance – even less than its southern Mediterranean cousins Greece, Italy and Portugal. It's a tendency that plays out in Spain's bustling plazas, where terraces are filled with friends gathered shoulder-to-shoulder, sipping cañas (beers) in the sunshine. Amparo Lasén, professor of sociology at Complutense University of Madrid, says that people in Spain tend to be more physically demonstrative than northern Europeans. "You notice more difference if you compare with Nordic countries or with England," she said. Perhaps it's not that Spaniards are more affectionate than people elsewhere, but that they're more comfortable showing it. Kissing in public isn't necessarily a grand romantic gesture; it's simply an accepted part of everyday life. Living arrangements may also play a part. Around 65% of Spain's population lives in flats – the highest proportion in the EU – while soaring property prices have made it increasingly difficult for young adults to move out of the family home. Lasén suggests that limited privacy at home can push intimate moments into public spaces. "In Spain we have this housing crisis, meaning that we are more used to meeting our friends outside – going to bars, going to restaurants – rather than doing it at our homes," she says, adding that couples now have to seek out a secluded bench for some alone time – or nearly alone, at least. But the housing crisis isn't the underlying reason for its public displays of affection, says Lasén. More important is the country's relaxed attitude towards them. "If no one gives you a bad look or just you don't care, well, that's the thing that makes it easier to have this kind of demonstration in public." Isabel Nieto Tous, 28, who moved back in with her parents three years ago after living abroad, knows how awkward dating without much privacy can be. "I didn't want to tell my parents I was staying at people's houses, because it was a bit awkward, so I would say I was staying at a friend's place," she said. Tous, who has lived in Japan, France, Germany and Tunisia, believes that dating is different in Spain; she says there's an instant warmth from the start. "People get very touchy and close very fast. Maybe you're in a situationship; you've met someone two times, and already you're holding hands in public and very touchy," she says. "I think kissing in public is very accepted in general," she adds. "There's no differentiation between indoors and outdoors. People behave the same way in the intimate space as they do in the outside space." While PDA may be a familiar sight in Spain today, expressions of sexuality were once tightly controlled. Under Francisco Franco’s dictatorship (1939-1975), conservative Catholic values and restrictive legislation dictated public behaviour, criminalising homosexuality and policing public displays of affection. Couples could even be fined for kissing in public. After Franco's death in 1975, Spain underwent a profound cultural transformation. In Madrid, the exuberant counterculture movement known as La Movida Madrileña celebrated freedom and self-expression, with film-makers such as Pedro Almodóvar challenging the conservative values of the past. As the movement flourished, affection and sexuality became increasingly visible in public life. But the sea-change didn't happen spontaneously. LGBT activists had been protesting for decades, clearing the path for a more open and accepting society. One pivotal protest took place in Madrid on 23 February 1987. The previous year, two women had been arrested for kissing in Madrid's Puerta del Sol and held in police custody for two days under the Escándalo Público (Public Scandal) law. Their detention promoted local campaign groups to organise a mass kiss-in to draw attention to the case. From that year until around the 1990s, every Pride March in Madrid finished with a kiss in Puerta del Sol. Kissing in the street had become a powerful act of peaceful protest, and the public-scandal offence was abolished in 1988. Today, public displays of affection can be seen across Spain, but that freedom isn't experienced equally. An older couple kissing on a public bench may attract more attention, while same-sex couples can face greater scrutiny, Lasén said. "Not everyone is equally comfortable showing their relationship." For Paula Furió, a former wedding photographer in Valencia, kissing is a symbol of something much bigger. "There's still work to do, but Spanish society in general is very open. Kissing is like the tip of the iceberg: it gives you a sense of the freedom you can have in Spain. It's an expression of freedom." It made me think back to my friend returning from Japan and the relief she felt at seeing a couple kissing on the bench. Perhaps she wasn't just happy to be home, she was happy to be in a country where authenticity overrules good manners. Maybe the most remarkable thing about kissing in Spain is how unremarkable it's become. – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: I Visited China as an American Without a Visa—Here’s How You Can Do It Too
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Last month, I visited China as an American—without going through a multi-week visa application process. This is thanks to a recent policy introduced in 2024 that allows certain travelers to visit China for a maximum of 10 days while transiting between one country and another. Though the rule can feel intimidating in theory, it’s relatively straightforward in practice as long as you prepare accordingly. Officially called the “240-Hour Visa-Free Transit Policy," the program is part of China’s goal to attract more inbound international travelers, according to Mei Zhang, the founder of WildChina and a Condé Nast Traveler travel specialist. “The idea is to make visiting China an easier decision,” Zhang says. “Most people are daunted by the idea of queuing for a visa at the Chinese consulate. Removing that step makes it easier for people to come.” And even though the policy is designed for transiting between countries, 10 days is still enough time for a meaningful visit. “Beyond the quick business visits or short stopovers people may associate with China, ten days gives travelers time to explore several destinations, experience the culture, and develop a deeper appreciation for the country,” says Catherine Heald, CNT specialist and founder of Remote Lands, which specializes in travel to Asia. However, because the program is relatively new, not all airline or airport staff are familiar with it—which almost resulted in me being denied boarding. To help you avoid ending up in a similar situation, here’s what travelers should know before booking your flight to China, so you too can see the Forbidden City in Beijing, the futuristic skyline glowing along the Bund in Shanghai, the terracotta warriors in Xi'an, and the mountainous megacity of Chongqing. What is China’s 10-day visa-free transit policy? Officially called the “240-Hour Visa-Free Transit Policy,” this new rule was first introduced by China’s National Immigration Administration in December 2024. It permits a traveler to visit China without obtaining a visa ahead of time as long as the total length of their stay in the country does not exceed 240 hours. “It’s a great policy that has driven the growth of international travelers to China,” says Zhang, “but you do need to read the fine print before using it.” The fine print: First of all, the operative word is transit. You have to enter China from one country, then leave it for another, different country. For example, flying from the US to China, then from China to Japan is allowed. However, going from the US to China, then back to the US, is not. Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan count as separate destinations for this policy, so a trip that goes from Hong Kong to mainland China to Taiwan would qualify for a visa-free transit in China that does not last longer than 10 days. Second: Only holders of passports from 57 countries, including the United States, can take advantage of this policy. See the full list here. And third: You have to enter and exit via designated ports. The full list is here, and it conveniently includes the cities you might visit on a first-time visit to China, like Beijing, Shanghai, and Chengdu. If you want to travel beyond the areas permitted by the transit policy, you’ll have to apply for a Chinese visa. “Remember that you can enter and leave through the same eligible Chinese city or choose different eligible cities,” says Heald of Remote Lands. So you could come to China through Shanghai, spend three days there, then take the high-speed train to Beijing, stay for another three days, then depart for a third destination like nearby South Korea to make the most out of your trip. How to plan a trip that qualifies for the 10-day visa-free transit policy To try the transit policy for myself, I kept my first-ever trip to China simple. I arrived in Shanghai on September 30 and departed on October 5, entering and exiting through the same qualifying port, Shanghai Pudong International Airport (PVG). I stayed in the country for a total of five nights, well under the 240-hour limit. (For what it’s worth, I stayed at the good-looking PuLi Shanghai, the very cool Upper House Shanghai, and the historically rich Capella Shanghai, Jian Ye Li, to explore different parts of the city.) I’m an American citizen, so my US passport made me eligible for the transit policy. As for my routing, I departed from Paris, where I live, on a direct flight to Shanghai; from there I flew onward to Manila. The logic is that this made my visit to China count as a long layover since my final destination was actually the Philippines. As you prepare your itinerary, check—and double check—that your passport, routing, entry and departure ports in China, and destinations within China all qualify under the 240-hour visa-free transit policy before you make your bookings. The list of qualifying passports and entry-exit ports in China can be found here. Once you have all your confirmation info, it’s a good idea to get organized and put together a folder with all your bookings as proof of your plans to stay no more than 10 days in China. “Carry printed copies of your confirmed onward tickets, hotel reservations, and itinerary,” Heald says. She also recommends calling your airline before departure and confirming your transit eligibility with them. You might even print the official page describing the policy (again, here!) so you can present it to anyone you encounter, like a check-in agent, who might be unfamiliar with the relatively new 10-day rule. Consider this your heads up, says Zhang: “It’s a great policy but sometimes the implementation on the ground can be uneven.” For an added layer of security, consider booking your travel to China with local tour operators or travel specialists like WildChina or Remote Lands. They can design a trip that will definitely qualify for the transit policy, and can help you out in case you run into issues while you’re traveling. How I nearly didn’t make it onto my flight to Shanghai Well, I did none of the above. I arrived at Paris-Charles de Gaulle for my flight to Shanghai without any printed confirmations of my onward ticket to Manila, my three hotel stays, or the official policy from the Chinese National Immigration Administration’s official website. The Air France check-in agent asked me to present my Chinese visa, which, of course, I did not have. I tried to explain in French that I could go to China through this new policy, but the agent insisted, “Non, c’est pas possible.” Foolishly, I plugged “10-day visa-free transit China” into Google on my phone and presented the results to him. He sighed, switched to English, and said, “That is not official. That is AI Overview.” I asked if there was anyone at Air France I could talk to, and the agent shook his head. Maybe he softened when he saw the panic creep across my face because he then phoned a colleague, an Air France agent who was Chinese. The other agent explained that I was correct, there is indeed a new 10-day transit policy, and all I had to do was present my onward ticket to the Philippines, which I did have saved as a screenshot on my phone. May my failure to properly prepare be your reminder to print out everything, including your flight and accommodation info, as well as the official visa-free transit policy. If there was ever a time to be a type-A traveler, it’s this. Arriving in China on the 10-day visa-free transit visa Once in China, the process becomes much smoother. All international travelers are required to fill out a digital arrival form, whether they have a visa or not. The form asks if you have a visa for China and, when you select no, offers a drop-down menu where you can declare that you are visiting through the 240-hour visa-free transit policy. Once that’s done, the form gives you a QR code that confirms you’ve completed the form; screenshot this code, just in case. Then go through the immigration line, approach the immigration officer, and present whatever is asked of you, like that QR code or your onward ticket, when prompted. That’s it! For my journey, I got to Pudong Airport in Shanghai, logged onto the airport Wi-Fi, completed the form, and went into the immigration line. They didn’t ask for the QR code but they did ask for my ticket to Manila. Once everything looked good to them, they stamped my passport with a transit visa—a little sticker that declared my date of entry into China and when they expected me to leave. I was cleared to go, and I stepped into the duty-free shopping area, located right before baggage claim, feeling giddy and satisfied that it all worked out. Zhang says working with a travel company could help relieve some of the stress on the arrival side too: “WildChina normally would book a VIP airport pickup if any of our travelers are using the 10-day transit visa. This way, an airport concierge would meet the guests at the gate and walk them through the visa step-by-step. This eases the stress of facing an unfamiliar bureaucratic process.” One of the things that greatly intimidated me about visiting China was how different the tech is. There’s no Uber or Google Maps, which has been very helpful for me on my solo travels in new-to-me countries. The very fine teams at PuLi Shanghai and Upper House Shanghai helped me get set up with the right apps, and I was zipping around the city in no time. (For a map app, Apple Maps worked like a charm, to my surprise.) Here are tips for what Chinese apps to download before traveling. First, set up Alipay, which is a do-it-all app and a total lifeline in China. You can link an international bank card and use it for all payments everywhere you go; call a DiDi car (China’s equivalent of Uber or Lyft), use its translation tool, and more. “Alipay is part of everyday life here,” Zhang says. “At most restaurants, you can scan the QR code on your table with Alipay, choose your dishes—already translated on the interface—and pay through the app.” Be sure to set it up and link your bank account or card before you arrive in China; some verification steps require authorization via your phone number, which you may not have access to while in the country. Second, everyone in China is on WeChat, so you’d do well to download that too; it’s how I communicated with the guest experiences team at Capella Shanghai, Jian Ye Li, who took me on cultural tours in the hotel’s neighborhood. Think of it as Chinese WhatsApp. And to stay connected online, Heald suggests checking if your existing carrier offers roaming in mainland China (helpful for any verification texts you may need to receive). Otherwise, get a compatible travel eSIM that explicitly covers it. A home carrier or a travel eSIM will allow you to connect to sites like Google Workplace and apps like Instagram that you would not be able to normally access through the internet while in China. For my phone, Airalo, a travel eSIM, and Free, my French home carrier, worked perfectly. “If you'll be using a laptop or tablet on Wi-Fi and need access to services such as Google, WhatsApp, or Instagram, install a VPN and arrange any paid subscription before you leave,” Zhang says. “Downloading and setting it up can be much trickier once you're in China.” I, for one, used Astrill VPN to stay connected on my laptop to sites like Gmail and YouTube. And finally, both Zhang and Heald recommend keeping an open mind. “China can feel very different from what you know,” Heald says. “Give yourself the chance to observe, ask questions and learn, rather than expecting everything to feel familiar.” Zhang adds, “That's part of getting to know a place. Don’t be afraid to ask for help or start a conversation, even if you only have a few words in common. You'll often find people are curious about you too, and pleased that you've come to see where they live.”

item.title: Singapore Airlines unveils the world's largest double bed in the sky as part of a £1.2 billion cabin makeover
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Getting a good night's sleep on a long-haul flight isn't always easy, even when you're lucky enough to be flying First Class. But Singapore Airlines is taking things to a whole new level, unveiling what it claims will be the largest double bed in commercial aviation, alongside a major revamp of its long-haul cabins. The airline announced on Friday 6 November that it is approximately £1.2 billion in redesigned cabins across all four travel classes, with the first aircraft expected to enter service in the second half of 2027. The biggest change is coming to First Class, where passengers travelling together will be able to transform two adjoining seats into a double bed measuring 203cm long and 152cm wide – larger than a standard UK double mattress. The seats can also be converted into a two-person sofa, while curved sliding doors and retractable dividers will offer additional privacy. And the luxury doesn't stop there. The new suites will feature Italian Poltrona Frau leather upholstery, personal wardrobes, dedicated dining spaces and 32-inch 4K entertainment screens. Passengers can also expect proper bedding, including cotton sheets, duvets, a choice of pillows and mattress toppers from German bedding specialist Paradies. Business Class passengers won't be left out either. Redesigned seats will come with sliding privacy doors, improved lumbar support and fully flat beds, with selected adjoining seats offering the option to sleep alongside a travelling companion. Smart controls in both premium cabins will even remember passengers' preferred seating positions for future flights. But what about those of us travelling further back? Premium Economy will benefit from additional personal space, adjustable leg rests, dedicated storage and larger entertainment screens. Meanwhile, Economy passengers can look forward to redesigned seats with more leg space, adjustable headrests and new storage compartments. The upgrades will be introduced gradually across Singapore Airlines' new Boeing 777-9 aircraft and 41 retrofitted Airbus A350-900 aircraft, including its ultra-long-range fleet. The latter will also receive First Class cabins for the first time. There's no confirmed date yet for when passengers will be able to try the new double beds, but one thing is certain: the prospect of sleeping at 35,000 feet has just become a little more appealing.

item.title: What to Expect at Boulder’s First Sundance Film Festival Coming January 2027
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Since 1985, the Sundance Film Festival has been showcasing independent films and drawing thousands of cinema-loving travelers to Park City, Utah. But starting in 2027, Sundance has a new home—the largest independent film festival in the country will be landing in Boulder, Colorado, from January 21 to 31. Boulderites should brace themselves for a massive influx of visitors; last year, Park City saw 85,472 in-person festival attendees. “The Sundance Film Festival outgrew Park City, maybe 10 or 15 years ago,” Boulder film commissioner Bruce Borowski says. “At some point they had to move just to accommodate the crowds and the success of the festival.” As a local, I’ve been able to witness the mounting anticipation firsthand. I was present at the celebratory press conference at Boulder Theater in March 2025 when Governor Jared Polis stated, “What excites me the most is that we are opening the door in Colorado for artists from across the world to showcase their stories and to become part of our story.” It’s a big win for the city both culturally and economically, but it’s also an opportunity for visitors to experience the all-around appeal of Boulder. Between attending film screenings and rubbing elbows with the filmmakers and actors in town, there are award-winning restaurants to enjoy, mountainous terrain to hike and ski, and can’t-miss tourist hot spots to explore. The decision to bring Sundance to Boulder was based largely on the city’s natural beauty and creative community, which align with the original vision of the festival. Aside from being home to Sundance founder Robert Redford’s alma mater, CU Boulder, the city’s walkable downtown and convenient location make it a great fit for the event. “Being located near an international airport, Boulder is really easy to get to,” explains Cris Jones, director of strategic partnerships for the city of Boulder “It’s right up against the mountains, and you get to have a mountain experience—without having to go over any mountain passes to get here.” Unlike the festival experience in Park City, where film screenings and activations were more spread out, the Boulder experience will be more centralized; all venues—which include Boulder Theater, Chautauqua Auditorium, and eTown Hall—will be within about a two-mile radius. “It’s more connected and accessible,” Paula DuPré Pesmen, managing director of festival and institute operations at Sundance Institute says. “It will be easy to get around from venue to venue, from panels to films, from restaurants to shops.” People can take advantage of dedicated Sundance Film Festival shuttles, along with free HOP bus service, shared e-bike passes, and free Regional Transportation District (RTD) transportation to and from Boulder. Once you’re downtown, most venues and activities are within walking distance of each other, and bus routes will encompass the hotels in Boulder to pick up and drop off festivalgoers. Along with the perks of having Sundance in Boulder, there are challenges expected as well, such as increased traffic and larger crowds at restaurants and businesses. And while Boulder has proven its capacity to host large events, the issue of lodging has come up. “The Boulder Creek Fest brings in over 90,000 people in one day, and the audience expected for Sundance is around 90,000 people over 11 days,” Charlene Hoffman, CEO of Visit Boulder, says. “The challenge that we’ve had, and that we’ve worked through for the most part, is the lodging component, because housing that many people over 11 days is new for us.” Hoffman shares that the city has helped residents in the community get their short-term rental licenses in order to rent out their homes. These listings can be found on Airbnb, Vrbo, and other home rental sites. Travelers are encouraged to look into lodging beyond Boulder County as well, such as Denver and Estes Park, both of which will be running free shuttles to Boulder. Whether you plan to attend screenings or not, there’s plenty to eat, drink, and do in Boulder as the inaugural festival kicks off. In between film screenings, recaffeinate at one of the many cafes in town, like Boulder-founded Ozo Coffee Roasters (located on both the east and west sides of Pearl Street). Or pop by my favorite coffee shop with a view, Spruce Confections on Pearl’s west end, and mingle with festivalgoers over fresh-baked pastries. “That’s always been the magic for me when going to the festival,” Pesmen says. “You find yourself in conversations with people in lines at coffee shops and restaurants, and you talk about things that you heard or a film that you saw.” With over 400 restaurants in Boulder, options range from gourmet dining to fast-casual, depending on how you’re feeling after a day of watching films. For upscale Northern Italian fare, make reservations at the Michelin-starred, James Beard Award-winning Frasca. Or grab a bite at The Sink, the more than 100-year-old institution on College Hill. Not only does it have the best burger in Boulder (I can vouch for this), but it was once the workplace of Sundance founder Robert Redford. In 1955, he was a CU Boulder student working as the restaurant’s janitor. Finally, cap off the night with cocktails at License No. 1, a speakeasy-themed lounge beneath the historic Hotel Boulderado. For creative tiki drinks and tropical decor, duck into Jungle and feel winter’s chill melt away. Boulder’s natural scenery—particularly the iconic Flatirons formations jutting from the foothills—is even more breathtaking when dusted in glittering snow. Play in the snow at Nederland’s Eldora Mountain Resort, just 21 miles from downtown Boulder. Catch the hourly Ski-n-Ride shuttle (a day pass costs $5.50) from Downtown Boulder Station to ski the slopes or snowshoe the Nordic Center’s groomed trails. Discuss film screenings on a crisp, invigorating hike through pine-scented air at Chautauqua Park (I’m partial to the Bluebell Mesa Trail). For a mellow walk with rewarding views of white-frosted peaks, meander along the Bobolink Trail on the south side of town. When you’re ready to head indoors, warm up with a hot beverage at the Dushanbe Teahouse and take in the beautifully intricate interior, which was crafted by artisans in Tajikistan, then shipped and assembled here in Boulder. Another tea attraction not to be missed: a tour of the Celestial Seasonings factory. Busy festival attendees in need of some relaxation can book a massage or facial at the St. Julien Spa. And of course, your time in Boulder isn’t complete without strolling the four-block outdoor pedestrian mall on Pearl Street, which will still be glowing with holiday lights. “Just being around during Sundance, even without a ticket, is a really great experience,” Hoffman says. “There’s so much energy.” Paige Triola has been a Boulder enthusiast since moving to the city in 2019. She wrote an exhaustive guide on Boulder for U.S. News & World Report, and is eager to see the Sundance Film Festival thrive in its new setting.

item.title: IDEA: Is Your Sodium Intake Impacting Your Hiking Performance? A Dietitian Explains Why It Matters.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Take a look at the nutrition label on a freeze-dried backpacking meal, and you might be surprised by how much sodium it contains. Some meals pack more than 1,500 mg into a single pouch, roughly two-thirds of the recommended daily limit of 2,300 mg for most adults. That’s a lot for one dinner, but when you’re spending hours sweating your way up steep climbs, you’re also losing sodium along with water. Sodium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal nerve and muscle function. Yet there’s a contradiction in how you might think about it on the trail: you question the sodium in your freeze-dried dinner while adding electrolyte powder to your water bottle and snacking on pretzels, jerky, and cheese. So, are you consuming too much sodium or not enough? The answer depends on what’s already in your food, how much you’re sweating, and how you’re replacing fluids. You can pack nearly identical amounts of food and end up with dramatically different sodium intakes. I compared two realistic days of backpacking food, each containing commercial meals, protein bars, snacks, and other familiar trail staples. Both provide roughly 3,150 calories and weigh about 23 ounces dry, yet one contains 5,465 mg of sodium while the other contains just 1,975 mg. That’s nearly 3,500 mg of difference before you add a single electrolyte packet. Some of the variation comes down to individual products: Mountain House Beef Lasagna contains 1,180 mg of sodium, compared with 340 mg in Good To-Go Pad Thai. Even switching pretzel flavors or protein bar brands can make a noticeable difference. Neither food bag is automatically better, but the comparison shows why it’s worth checking what you’re already carrying before deciding to supplement. Health experts recommend limiting sodium for a reason. Consistently consuming more than your body needs can raise blood pressure, increasing your risk of heart disease and stroke over time. A particularly salty meal can also leave you thirsty or temporarily bloated as your body regulates its fluid balance. If you’ve been advised to limit sodium because of high blood pressure, kidney disease, or another medical condition, those recommendations still matter when you’re backpacking. But eating a high-sodium diet day after day isn’t necessarily the same as eating salty meals during a strenuous backpacking trip. When you’re sweating heavily, you lose sodium you wouldn’t lose while sitting at a desk. That doesn’t mean every milligram of sodium in your food is necessary, or that you should add electrolytes without thinking about what you’re already eating. It simply means your activity and conditions matter when interpreting those numbers on the label. Even if you’re hiking alongside someone on the same trail, you may be losing very different amounts of sodium. Sweat losses depend on two things: how much you sweat and how concentrated that sweat is. Research has found sweat sodium concentrations ranging from roughly 230 to 1,600 mg per liter. Temperature, exertion, clothing, heat acclimatization, and individual physiology all affect your losses, which means mileage alone tells you very little about how much sodium you’ve lost. Here’s another wrinkle: losing 800 mg of sodium through sweat doesn’t automatically mean you need to consume 800 mg to replace it. Your body regulates sodium and water balance, and research suggests targeted sodium replacement matters more under certain combinations of prolonged exercise, substantial sweat losses, and fluid replacement. That’s why taking an electrolyte packet every hour isn’t necessarily appropriate. A packet doesn’t account for how much you’re sweating, how much you’re drinking, or how much sodium you’re getting from food. Sodium doesn’t have to come from an electrolyte supplement to count. Salty snacks, meals, and electrolyte drinks all contribute to your intake, although when you consume that sodium can matter during long, sweaty days. Imagine spending ten hours hiking in warm weather, sweating heavily and drinking water but eating very little. At camp, you prepare a freeze-dried dinner containing 1,500 mg of sodium. That sodium helps replace losses and retain fluids during recovery, but it wasn’t available during the preceding hours of hiking. Eating salty snacks throughout a prolonged, sweaty hike provides some sodium along the way instead of waiting until dinner. That doesn’t mean you need electrolyte powder in every water bottle. If you’re regularly eating pretzels, cheese, jerky, or other salty foods, you’re already consuming sodium during the day. On the other hand, if your trail menu contains relatively little sodium or you struggle to eat while hiking, an electrolyte drink may be a convenient alternative. What matters isn’t whether the sodium comes from a packet or a snack, but whether you’re adding something your food isn’t already providing. It’s easy to assume that replacing the sodium you lose through sweat will protect you from exercise-associated hyponatremia (EAH), a potentially dangerous drop in blood sodium. But according to the Wilderness Medical Society, most cases occur primarily because you drink too much fluid relative to your losses, often combined with your body’s tendency to retain water during prolonged exercise. Sweat sodium losses can contribute under some circumstances, but taking electrolyte supplements won’t prevent hyponatremia if you’re overdrinking. The guidelines recommend avoiding overdrinking, generally by drinking according to thirst or using fluid needs you’ve estimated from experience in similar conditions. They also recommend having salty foods or drinks available during long, hot activities. Headaches, fatigue, nausea, and muscle cramps aren’t reliable indicators that you need more sodium because they can have several causes. If you or a hiking partner develops worsening confusion, repeated vomiting, seizures, or collapses during or after prolonged exertion, seek urgent medical help rather than assuming more water or electrolytes will solve the problem. There’s no simple answer. Your sweat losses vary with the conditions and your individual physiology. Even knowing exactly how much sodium you lose wouldn’t tell you how much to replace. For context, 1,500 mg per day is considered an adequate intake for most adults under ordinary conditions, while 2,300 mg is the general recommended daily limit. Neither is a backpacking-specific target. A food bag containing 5,465 mg isn’t automatically excessive for a strenuous hiking day, just as one containing 1,975 mg isn’t necessarily inadequate. And since research hasn’t consistently shown that extra sodium improves endurance performance, there’s little reason to chase a precise replacement target. The bottom line? Hike your own hike. If you’re curious about your sodium intake, track what you eat and drink, the conditions you’re hiking in, and how you feel during and afterward. You might notice patterns that help you plan future trips, without getting caught up in replacing every milligram of sodium you sweat out. Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: IDEA: Explore California’s scenic North Coast on low-intensity cycling route
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune
Soon after setting off on a 90-mile journey along Northern California’s Pacific Coast Bicycle Route, fog cocooned U.S. Route 101. At the crest of the morning’s climb, the sun burned through and our surroundings took shape. As my travel partner, Jess, and I pedaled down the other side, a scene we had hoped for when imagining this ride opened before us. Sea stacks the size of city blocks rose from the ocean. A hint of mist floated across cliffs protecting driftwood-strewed beaches below. A baby-blue sky drew a horizontal line atop the glittering Pacific. Inland, purple lupines and yellow poppies fluttered along this portion of 101 known as the Redwood Highway. Immediately beyond, the forest beckoned. When we started dreaming of this trip months ago — before deciding on California — Jess requested we make it about discovery, not intense, all-day rides. “I’d like to cycle a coast with lots of nature,” Jess said as we researched routes. “No big cities. It should be easy to follow with cool spots to stay. Inside, no tents! And good food. Rides short enough to reach our destinations by lunch but long enough to earn wine each night.” The winner, this section of the Pacific Coast Bicycle Route, would take us on a four-stop adventure from Crescent City south to Klamath, Trinidad and Eureka. We would average around 30 miles per day. (In total, the 1,862-mile route extends from Vancouver to the Mexican border.) We’d ride gravel bikes, which combine the geometry of road bikes with mountain-bike sturdiness, and load them with bags containing tools, toiletries and necessary clothes. As a bonus, cycling the North Coast meant we’d ride in 55- to 60-degree temperatures during our trip in June. We arrived in Crescent City, the start of our itinerary, a day early to gather supplies and sightsee. What we knew was that this former shipping hub (fueled by the 1850s gold rush, and then lumber) was the site, in 1964, of California’s worst tsunami. What we discovered was a working-class vibe surrounded by secluded beaches and seductive sunsets. Today’s Crescent City — often called Comeback Town, USA, for its post-tsunami resilience — is perhaps best known as the headquarters of the Redwood National and State Parks and as base camp for hikes through ancient forests in Jedediah Smith Redwoods State Park and Del Norte Coast Redwoods State Park. After dropping our gear at a rented house, we cycled along the shore into town. Seals and sea lions basked around Crescent City’s harbor, unfazed by fishermen or patrons of nearby restaurants. For lunch at the SeaQuake brewery, we ordered fish and chips made with local, panko-crusted rockfish and washed it down with Redwood Highway Hazy IPA. We then wheeled over to the headquarters of Redwoods National and State Parks, of which Prairie Creek Redwoods State Park, which we’d soon ride through, was one. Inside, rangers answered questions about hikes and places to sleep. When I asked about biking the North Coast, Kyle Achziger, a nature guide at Prairie Creek told me, “Cycling is a great way to experience the redwoods because it forces you to be focused and engaged.” In other words, it forces you to slow down. We had no choice but to slow down on that first foggy morning. After 5 miles of flat road, the route ascended more than 1,200 pedal-mashing feet. And though there was a shoulder and “Share the Road” signs, we rode with greater caution because of cars. Still, riding the 101 to reach redwood parks is a rite of passage. The route and the parks grew up together. The 101 was among the country’s first numbered highways when commissioned a century ago, in 1926, and the three redwood state parks were established between 1923 and 1929. (Since 1994, Redwood National Park, created in 1968, and the state parks have cooperatively managed this four-park, 130,000-plus-acre system.) Outside Klamath, our day’s goal, we stopped at Trees of Mystery, an 80-year-old roadside attraction that mixes redwood worship and vintage Americana. We stashed our bikes behind a 49-foot-tall Paul Bunyan and his blue ox, Babe, which loomed over the parking lot, and hit the trails looping through 120 acres of trees (the largest nearly 300 feet high and 19 feet wide). We then climbed stairs to the Redwood Canopy Trail, which wound us along suspension bridges connecting 100-feet-high viewing platforms. In Klamath proper, the administrative center of the Yurok Tribe, we cycled to the Yurok Country Visitor Center to join a redwood canoe tour on the Klamath River. In the fall of 2024, after the largest dam removal in history, this 263-mile waterway — which flows from Klamath Falls, Ore., to Klamath, Calif., where it meets the Pacific Ocean — again ran free. For the first time since World War I, Chinook salmon were spawning near the river’s source. As egrets watched, Kobe Mitchell, our Yurok guide, paddled our century-old dugout canoe along redwood-lined banks. “Our culture is our way of life, our way of living, and that has always started from our river,” he said. Back on our bikes, we rode 3 miles to the Yurok-owned, 15-room Historic Requa Inn. Built in 1914 as a lodge for fishermen near the mouth of the Klamath, the inn still has a pre-dam-era homeyness. After tea in the living room’s overstuffed armchairs, we trekked up 600 feet to the Klamath River Overlook and stared down at a sandbar, spotlighted in the setting sun. To one side, the reborn Klamath lapped the sand, meeting its end. On the other, ocean waves crashed, welcoming a new beginning. The next morning, as we gathered our gear for the 40-mile stage to Trinidad, I asked Jess how she felt. “Great,” she said, adding, “I like how cycling is part physical challenge and part logistics wrangling: food, packing, places to stay.” Indeed, there’s satisfaction in self-sufficiency: devising the route, understanding your limits. Thankfully, puzzling out such details has become easier. Navigation apps like Ride With GPS, AllTrails and Ride Club from the bicycle company Trek make it simple to create an itinerary. I purchased our digital and paper Pacific Coast maps from the Montana-based Adventure Cycling Association, North America’s largest cycling membership organization. Near the northern edge of Humboldt County and the Prairie Creek Redwoods State Park, the route split from the highway on to the Newton B. Drury Scenic Parkway. (They reconnect 10 miles later.) Cars slowed to a trickle as the road plunged into old-growth forests. We glided around curves, got off our bikes and sat on a soft bed of fallen needles in a patch of sunlight slanting between massive trunks. “The redwoods, once seen, leave a mark or create a vision that stays with you always,” the author John Steinbeck wrote. “From them comes silence and awe.” Around lunchtime, Trinidad rolled into view. Perched among redwoods, the town, which was founded in 1850 and now has a population of fewer than 400, felt like a village with its compact grid of cottages, galleries and shops. The streets sloped down to bluffs, forming a natural amphitheater overlooking Trinidad Bay. We walked to this amphitheater’s main stage: the Trinidad Head, a promontory of forested igneous rock rising 350 feet above the water. The 1.8-mile Trinidad Head Trail ringed the peninsular headland, taking us past the 155-year-old Trinidad Head Lighthouse and through tunnels of scrub oak that led to commanding views of the Pacific and enormous sea stacks. We celebrated our route’s penultimate evening at the Trinidad Bay Eatery. Locals clinked pints at the counter in the 51-year-old diner as waiters crowded our booth’s table with local oysters, clam chowder, shrimp and chips, a salad with Dungeness crab and sauvignon blanc from the nearby Moonstone Crossing Winery. We clinked our glasses: “Earning our wine.” Fog again cocooned us as we left Trinidad. Unlike the first morning, this last stage to Eureka would mostly take scenic drives, quiet streets and paths that paralleled the 101. The route out of town followed the North Coast’s indented coastline around spits of land poking into the mist and to the edge of sheer drops. Blue skies greeted us 20 miles later in Arcata, where the farmers’ market in the main plaza was in festival mode. Face-painted children ran between couples carrying baskets of greens, and college kids danced to a band. After coffee and muffins, we began our final 7-mile push on a just-opened section of the Humboldt Bay Trail along Arcata Bay’s shore to downtown Eureka, where Victorian architecture nonchalantly housed cafes, shops and hair salons. After checking into the Carter House Inns, we sat at the bar and ordered an opening libation from the hotel’s cellar of 3,800 wines. There’d be time enough to explore tomorrow. We’d visit the Dick Taylor Craft Chocolate factory, lounge in Eureka Books and take a tour of Humboldt Bay on the Madaket, the country’s oldest still-working passenger vessel. At this moment, we had nowhere to ride and all morning to sleep off the fog.

item.title: What Travelers Should Know About the Galápagos Floods—and the Ongoing Impact of El Ñino
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
On October 30 and 31, 2026, torrential rainfall on the Galápagos's Santa Cruz island caused waterways to overflow, flooding neighborhoods, damaging homes, and disrupting essential infrastructure. The local government declared an emergency, with over 2,000 people affected by the damage. This places the Galápagos among several beloved tourism destinations that are already grappling with the effects of El Ñino. The news has also left many travelers wondering: Is it safe to travel to the Galápagos right now? And how should those with upcoming cruises and hotel stays proceed? Rodrigo Jácome, who runs La K-leta Guest House and a small coffee farm on Santa Cruz, which is the archipelago's main inhabited island and a central hub for tourism, says the flooding has not damaged key tourism infrastructure—though it devastated other local livelihoods. “The flooding affected residential neighborhoods that are not particularly close to the main hotel areas,” says Jácome, who lost most of his coffee harvest in the rains. For those with upcoming travel, and locals who rely on travelers to make a living, however, “tourism operations resumed within days.” Authorities have reopened most visitor sites in the Galápagos National Park, and transportation has resumed, though conditions remain subject to change. Below, we report on all of the impacted areas across the Galápagos, which tours may be rerouted, and how to stay up on the news as future weather develops, according to those on the ground. Plus, local tour operators share advice on planning accordingly for trips in the months ahead. Which areas of the Galápagos were affected by the flooding? Santa Cruz is where you'll find many hotels, restaurants, tour operators, and transportation connections, and the area that experienced the most significant damage. Santa Cruz serves as a major base for day trips and cruises to other islands. Most visitors arriving by air fly in via neighboring Baltra, where the airport is located. Puerto Ayora, the island's main town, and the highland parish of Bellavista, were among the affected areas. Floodwaters damaged homes and roads, disrupted water and electricity services, and forced families to evacuate. The flooding also affected transportation infrastructure connecting Santa Cruz to Baltra Airport, the main gateway for visitors arriving by air to Santa Cruz. The road reopened on November 5 and reconstruction work is being carried out in parallel, allowing travelers to continue arriving to the island as planned. Although the emergency was concentrated in Santa Cruz, other islands also experienced heavy rainfall and localized flooding. Whitman Cox, a Galápagos National Park naturalist guide based in San Cristóbal, which is known for its sea lion colonies, volcanic landscapes, and popular snorkeling and diving sites, says there was no such damage in San Cristobal, but access to some of the beaches around the island has been restricted as weather conditions change. Travelers should therefore check conditions for all destinations on their itinerary, across the archipelago, rather than assuming all islands have been affected equally. Constant communication with tour guides, your hotel, or cruise line is the best way to get up-to-date information. Is it safe to visit the Galápagos right now? As of November 9, flights to Baltra and San Cristóbal were operating on their regular schedules, according to local reporting. Tourism activities have also continued, although some visitor sites remain temporarily closed. The Galápagos National Park has progressively reopened areas following safety assessments: As of November 9, Playa El Garrapatero in Santa Cruz was accessible again, while popular visitor sites Las Grietas, El Chato, and El Puntudo remained restricted. In San Cristóbal, La Lobería and Punta Carola had reopened, while surfing spots Puerto Chino and Playa Baquerizo remained closed. The Los Humedales sector in Isabela also remained closed. From November 9-18, Tortuga Bay, a beach in Santa Cruz, will be closed as a preventative measure due to tide changes. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office updated its Ecuador travel advisory on November 1 to include the flooding on Santa Cruz. It advises travelers to follow local authorities' instructions, avoid flooded areas, and confirm travel arrangements with airlines and tour operators. Cox emphasizes that travelers shouldn't panic—El Niño is a natural weather cycle. “People can still come. We shouldn't frighten them," says Cox. His main guidance is to be patient. “They may encounter transportation difficulties between certain points, which could take additional time.” He adds that the park has done its best in the interest of safety by closing the above sites as a precautionary measure. What is El Niño, and how else could it affect your trip? The flooding comes as Ecuador experiences an El Niño event, a climate phenomenon characterized by unusually warm ocean temperatures across the equatorial Pacific, which can alter atmospheric circulation and rainfall patterns. In Ecuador, El Niño is often associated with heavier rainfall, particularly along the coast and in the Galápagos. However, its effects vary by region and over time. According to the National Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology (INAMHI), the El Niño event remained active and was strengthening for the upcoming months with weather reports suggesting that heavy rainfall may last until February 2027. The potential implications for travelers include heavy rain, temporary road closures, changes to boat excursions, and restricted access to natural visitor sites. Weather conditions can also affect marine activities and inter-island transportation. However, this is not the first time El Niño has impacted the islands, and tour guides understand how to prepare. “It is a cyclical part of nature that we have seen every 10-15 years,” says Charles Wittmer, president of the Association of Boat Operators in the Galápagos, ADATUR. “Nature is unpredictable and if anything, this is a chance to see the adaptations of animals to changing weather conditions,” he says. “Remember: this is a natural laboratory of evolution.” On the wildlife front, Wittmer mentions that Galápagos penguins and cormorants adapt to warming ocean waters. And there's a plus: These shifts in marine ecosystem activity may increase the variety of species spotted while snorkeling. How should travelers prepare for a trip to the Galápagos during El Ñino? If you have an upcoming trip, local tourism specialists recommend staying informed and remaining flexible. It’s best to ask about excursion alternatives when booking a tour in the islands, should weather create the need to pivot. Before departure, confirm your flights and accommodation directly with your airline and tour operator. Ask whether your planned excursions are operating as anticipated and whether alternative activities are available if certain visitor sites are closed. Ask your tour guide for updates daily. It's also a good idea to purchase travel insurance that covers weather-related disruptions, medical emergencies, and unexpected accommodation or transportation expenses. Travelers can monitor official updates from INAMHI and the Galápagos National Park social media and from their website with forecasts, and plan smart by allowing extra flexibility in travel connections and excursions. Remember to also pack lightweight rain protection and waterproof bags for electronics and important documents. Like Cox, Wittmer emphasizes that nature is out of our control. “People should bring clothing and be ready for heavier rainfall and be flexible in their expectations.” How can travelers support local communities in the Galápagos? Whether staying in local communities, visiting for a few hours on cruise excursions, or simply passing through in transit, travelers contribute to the livelihoods of local businesses and workers, many of whom are also dealing with the consequences of the flooding, simply by visiting. As Jácome puts it, “Tourism is needed now more than ever to help rebuild the communities that lost everything.” Consider booking locally owned accommodation, hiring licensed local guides, eating at independent restaurants, and purchasing goods from small businesses. As always, travelers should also be mindful that affected neighborhoods are not tourist attractions. Avoid visiting damaged homes or taking photographs of residents dealing with the aftermath of the flooding without their permission. If you are traveling to Galápagos right now, consider packing water purification tablets, basic first-aid supplies, and hygiene kits to done to affected families (your guide or hotel can assist with routing these to the right place). You can also check with local emergency centers or your tour operator upon arrival to donate pet food or clean clothes directly to the most impacted neighborhoods. If you want to contribute to recovery efforts from afar, several organizations and initiatives have mobilized support: Fundación Charles Darwin: The foundation is part of an emergency fundraising initiative, with proceeds directed to the Santa Cruz emergency response committee (COE) to support urgent community needs. San Francisco de Quito University: The University has established a SOS Galapagos fund, collecting donations on their campus in Quito. They also have a donations link. Fundación Torraja: This local organization is administering a Community Kitchen and providing meals and donations directly to families who lost their belongings in the floods.

item.title: REVIEW: I just sailed the Nile on a Viking ship. It's a great way to tour Egypt
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Our Viking guide, Karim Zohny, is leading us through one of the best-preserved ancient temples in all of Egypt, the Temple of Hathor, explaining the famously colorful reliefs that line its massive sandstone pillars, walls and ceilings. Located along the Nile near the Egyptian city of Qena, it is, as Zohny notes, unusual in its motifs, which include intricate celestial maps and giant images of the Egyptian queen Cleopatra and her son Caesarion. That our small group of two dozen passengers from the Viking river ship Viking Osiris is even here is also relatively unusual. Most vessels that sail the Nile don’t come this far north. Instead, they stick to the 130-mile stretch of river that runs between the more southerly cities of Luxor and Aswan. It's just one of several things that make Viking's 11-night Egypt tours, in my opinion at least (after years of traveling in Egypt), among the best choices for exploring the country's splendors. Pairing a seven-night Nile sailing with four nights of land-based travel, Viking’s “Pharaohs and Pyramids” trips offer some of the most comprehensive, in-depth touring that you will find in Egypt. They also offer a Nile river ship experience that has few rivals, thanks to Viking’s recent rollout of an all-new series of Nile vessels that is setting a new bar for the region. In addition, as I have seen on more than one Viking trip in Egypt, the trips offer a particularly seamless and mostly all-inclusive experience, with just about every element — from lodging and meals to expert-led guided tours and special access to iconic sites — included in the fare. Aimed at the same sort of history-loving travelers who get excited about visiting the ancient ruins of Greece and Italy, Viking’s Egypt trips — like many tours of the country — focus heavily on what some consider the greatest civilization of all time: ancient Egypt. Indeed, almost from the moment we land in Cairo to begin the tour, which begins with a three-night stay at the upscale Fairmont Nile City Hotel, we are thrust more than 4,500 years back in time to one of the oldest and greatest eras of ancient Egypt: The Old Kingdom. Also known as the Age of the Pyramids, this was the period that saw the construction of monumental structures such as the 4,700-year-old Step Pyramid of Djoser, which we visit on our first full day of touring. Located at the edge of the desert just outside Cairo, in an area known as Saqqara, it was, as Zohny explains, not only the first pyramid built in Egypt but also by far the largest stone structure built by humans up to that time. In that respect, its construction was one of the great milestones of history. It's a history we experience viscerally as we frog-walk down a low-sloping tunnel into another nearby pyramid built for the pharaoh Teti. After nearly a hundred feet, we emerge into a three-room tomb covered in ancient hieroglyphics, among the oldest funerary texts ever found in an Egyptian tomb. The next day, Zohny, an expert “Egyptologist” who will be our guide for the entire trip, brings us to the even bigger (and more famous) Pyramids of Giza and the nearby Great Sphinx, which also are just outside of Cairo. Built about a century after the Step Pyramid of Djoser, the Giza pyramids mark the peak of pyramid building in Egypt and are truly a sight to behold. In between visiting these massive structures, we are treated to a full morning of exploring the new Grand Egyptian Museum, where we marvel at the gilded treasures recovered from the pharaoh Tutankhamun's tomb just a century ago. We also visit Cairo's alabaster-clad Mosque of Muhammad Ali. It is a whirlwind two days that prepare us for the equally stunning sites from the more recent New Kingdom, Ptolemaic and Roman periods of ancient Egypt that we will see while sailing the Nile on Viking Osiris. But first, we must get to the ship. Like most of the vessels that sail the Nile, Viking Osiris is based in Luxor, hundreds of miles south of Cairo — the center of ancient Egypt, which began around 4,100 years ago (when it was called Thebes). After checking out of the Fairmont, we fly as a group to Luxor on a charter flight. To sail the Nile on Viking Osiris or one of its many sister vessels (at last count, there were eight on the river) is to be on something akin to a greatest hits tour of nearly 2,000 years of iconic Egyptian structures. Luxor, Qena, Kom Ombo, Edfu. On the ship's weeklong itineraries, these Nile river destinations famous for ancient sites come one after the other, each offering something spectacular that you probably remember from your second-grade history class. In Luxor, it is the massive Temple of Karnak, with its colossal sandstone columns arranged in neat rows (if you’ve seen the James Bond vs. Jaws chase scene in the 1977 film “The Spy Who Loved Me,” you know what I’m talking about). In Qena, it is the impressive Temple of Hathor, which is part of an even bigger archeological site known as the Dendera Temple Complex. In Kom Ombo, it is the equally impressive temple of the same name, built during the Greco-Roman period and featuring reliefs of the Roman emperors Tiberius and Domitian. Then there’s Edfu, home to the long-buried-in-sand Temple of Horus. Lost to time until a French archeologist began digging it out 166 years ago, it is almost completely intact, with its hypostyle halls and inner sanctuary looking much as they did 2,000 years ago. Some of these destinations that the ship visits are gateways to multiple world-class sites. In addition to the Temple of Karnak (where Viking ships have an exclusive dock location), Luxor is our base for an outing to the nearby pharaonic burial grounds, the Valley of the Kings, a highlight of any Egypt tour. In our case, the visit includes the opportunity to descend into five of the more than 60 tombs found in the valley so far — two more than is typical for many Egypt tours. Viking has paid extra to get us access to perhaps the most famous tomb of them all, that of the pharaoh Tutankhamun (King Tut, as we called him when I was a boy), who remains inside the tomb in mummified form, as well as the spectacular (and normally expensive to visit) tomb of Seti I. During our stay in Luxor, we also wandered through the Temple of Luxor and the terraced Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut — the latter a masterpiece of ancient architecture. Some passengers also soar skyward in a hot air balloon (one of the few extra-charge excursions during the trip) for views of the Mortuary Temple, Valley of the Kings and other area sites from the air. While exploring the remnants of ancient Egypt is a big part of the trip, it’s not the only focus. As we sail the Nile, we also get a taste of everyday life on the river. Some of my favorite moments of the voyage come as we steam through the many rural stretches of the Nile between Luxor and Aswan, where the riverbanks often are lined with date palms, reeds, wild grasses and, in some areas, lush agricultural crops. It is a scene evoking the Nile of ancient times. At times, I spot farmers working in small fields of bananas or sugarcane, or tending to cows grazing along the waterfront. We regularly pass fishermen in small boats slapping the water with oars to scare the fish into nets — a traditional technique. It is, notably, a narrow band of abundance. In some places, the fertile area fed by the life-giving waters of the Nile stretches just a few hundred feet inland, in other places maybe a mile or two, before the landscape abruptly transforms into harsh desert that stretches for hundreds of miles. It’s one of the things that makes Egypt so fascinating. It is a country that essentially unfolds along one very long, very narrow ribbon of green in a sea of desert. Or, as the Greek historian Herodotus famously wrote, Egypt is the gift of the Nile. You can read about this in books, of course. But it's something you only truly understand when you see it up close from the deck of a passing vessel. One of the big allurements of Viking sailings on the Nile is their laid-back pace. Many Egypt tour itineraries include only three or four nights of cruising between Luxor and Aswan to see the major sites, or even fewer, resulting in a frenetic touring schedule. There is a lot to pack into just a few days. Viking is one of just a small number of Egypt tour companies that slow the Nile-cruising portion of the trip by spreading it over a seven-night span. This allows for not only a more in-depth experience but also a more relaxed one — the latter of which has particular appeal to the mostly older travelers who are Viking's core market. Many of Viking's customers are retirees who have the time for longer trips and also prefer to "explore the world in comfort," as Viking likes to say. On several days of the sailing, notably, we only tour ancient sites for a few hours in the morning and spend the afternoon relaxing on board as the vessel sails the river. During this time, Zohny and two other onboard Egyptologists lecture on topics such as medicine in ancient Egypt and Egyptian hieroglyphics. There are lessons in Egyptian cooking and basic Arabic. There's afternoon tea. But there’s also plenty of time to just kick back on the sun deck. The extra days also allow time for visits to ancient sites that most tours don’t include and for experiencing more on land than just ancient sites. In addition to stopping at lesser-visited Qena to see the Temple of Hathor, for instance, we spend a morning docked in the often overlooked Nile town of Esna to see not just its lovely if small Roman-era Temple of Khnum but to shop in one of its small markets for local textiles. For many of us, the shopping time allows us to haggle for Egyptian galabeyas — a traditional, loose-fitting robe worn by men and women across Egypt — for another major moment of the cruise, that night’s Taste of Egypt & Galabeya Evening. Passengers are encouraged to wear local dress, as the crew does, too, for a special dinner of all-local cuisine, and local music and entertainment. In Aswan, which is as far south as river ships on these itineraries can go, we spend two days experiencing a wide variety of activities that range from touring the dedicated-to-Isis Temple of Philae and sailing in a traditional wind-powered felucca to visiting one of the local villages that are home to Nubians — a distinct ethnic group that has been living in the region for thousands of years. We also visit the mighty 56-year-old Aswan High Dam, a marvel of construction that blocks river ships from going farther south on the Nile. As noted above, Viking Osiris is part of a new series of Viking vessels on the Nile that, in my opinion, are the best-designed on the river. Upscale and intimate, with just 41 cabins and suites apiece, these vessels feature the same elegant, clean-lined Scandinavian-influenced décor that can be found on Viking ships around the world and lots of high-end touches. Public areas on each vessel include a stylish restaurant overseen by a European chef, a casual deck-top eatery with indoor and outdoor seating, and a cozy lounge and bar — all offering commanding views. A key element of the design is the wide expanses of clear glass that serve as the outward-facing walls of nearly every public room. This essentially turns the entire ship into a window onto the stunning, colorful scenery that is scrolling by. In essence, the light-greenish water of the Nile, the rich green papyrus and tall bamboo-like grasses along its banks, and the tan desert cliffs in the distance become the "art" and focal points of the ship's spaces. That the glass is clear is notable for the Nile, where many vessels are wrapped in dark or metallic glass to reflect the often-intense heat of the sun — glass that, alas, often makes these ships feel closed off to the splendors of the river. Viking went to great lengths to keep the view clear by sourcing a more expensive type of glass that blocks heat without appearing tinted from the inside — a seemingly small detail that makes all the difference. Other public spaces on each ship include a swanky sun deck with rows of plush lounge chairs for sunning and lovely shaded seating areas. At the very back of the top deck is a narrow pool.
Even the smallest cabins on the ships are generous in size, measuring 232 square feet. And they are filled with luxury elements such as high-end linens and pillows on the beds, heated bathroom floors and roomy wardrobes with wooden hangers. My cabin — one of eight suites measuring 409 square feet or more — was among the most luxurious that I have seen on a Nile ship. Modern and residential in feel, it featured a large living room with a seating area and desk for working, an adjacent bedroom with a walk-in closet and bathroom, and an outdoor balcony with seating for two. The latter is something you don't always see on Nile ships. Still, perhaps the most upscale touch of the vessel is the service level that it offers. A crew of 48 people is on hand to serve at most 82 passengers (the ship's maximum capacity with every cabin full — on my sailing, there were just 72), so there's never a lack of staff to cater to your every whim. I saw this high service level firsthand quite a few times on board, whether it be from the waiter in the restaurant who, unprompted, prepared my traveling companion a special soothing tea with ginger, lime and honey after she mentioned she was feeling a little queasy, to the bartender in the lounge who not only remembered my favorite cocktail but started mixing it before I even had to ask. In addition, Zohny, our Egyptologist, was the most knowledgeable and engaging Egypt guide that I have encountered during 25 years of visiting the country. As is typical for higher-end tours of Egypt, Viking's trips in the region aren't inexpensive. Sold as a combined land-and-cruise tour package, the 11-night "Pharaohs and Pyramids" journeys start at $6,999 per person, based on double occupancy (about $14,000 for a couple sharing a room). And such starting fares are specifically for packages that include an entry-level "standard" cabin without a balcony during the cruise portion of the trip. For a package that includes a cabin with a balcony during the cruise portion of the trip, you'll find starting rates of around $7,499 per person (about $15,000 per couple). Packages that include a stay in a larger suite cost closer to $25,000 per couple or more, depending on the departure date. In general, you'll also pay more at all cabin levels for departures from late December through early April, when cooler temperatures in Egypt make touring more pleasant. That said, such fares are highly all-inclusive. Not only are your ship and hotel rooms included in the price, but most of your meals (along with wine, beer and soft drinks with lunch and dinner while on the ship).
