You also get extensive guided tours to all the main sites every day of your trip. The latter is a significant value, given the cost and logistical headaches of booking tours in Egypt on your own. Indeed, a notable part of what you're paying for on a Viking trip to Egypt is access to extremely knowledgeable Egypt experts (known as Egyptologists) who travel with you and explain the many ancient temples, tombs and other historic sites you're seeing. In addition, the fares include the interior flights in Egypt that will get you between Cairo and Luxor for the cruise portion of the trip, as well as airport transfers when you book international flights through Viking. Some higher-level cabins also come with complimentary laundry service and a premium beverage package. Little things like shipboard WiFi are also included for all. Viking's 11-night "Pharaohs and Pyramids" tours offer one of the most comprehensive and seamless ways to explore Egypt. The trips pair a well-paced, seven-night Nile sailing aboard an exceptionally designed new ship with a multi-night land stay in Cairo, together allowing visits to many of Egypt's most iconic attractions, including the Pyramids of Giza and the Valley of the Kings. While fares are on the higher side among Egypt tours, the extensive all-inclusive nature of the trips — accommodations, most meals, extensive touring with an expert Egyptologist and internal flights are among the inclusions — means they offer a lot of value for the money. item.title: Where was 'Rivals' season 2 filmed? The picturesque real-life locations behind the hit Disney+ series
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we look at Rivals filming locations. When Rivals hit the small screen in October 2024, it didn't take long for it to become a national phenomenon. The stellar cast – which includes household names David Tennant, Aidan Turner, and Alex Hassell – stole hearts and sparked fury with their portrayal of the dramas playing out between locals living in the bucolic English countryside. Set in 1986, in the charming, chocolate-box (fictional) village of Rutshire, in the Cotswolds, MP Rupert Campbell-Black (Hassell) is embroiled in a fiery rivalry with Lord Tony Baddingham (Tenant), owner of independent TV station Corinium. The first season followed the feud while also delving into the family dynamics of Declan O'Hara (Turner), star of Corinium's talk show, as his daughter, Taggie (played by Bella Maclean), starts to fall in love with new neighbour and womaniser Rupert… The much-anticipated second season of the Disney+ show was released on Friday 15 May 2026. Viewers delved headfirst into the continued battle between the show's stars, as the rivals became increasingly frantic and desperate to destroy their opponents. All of this is, of course, against the backdrop of ’80s glamour and excess, with decadent parties, hedonistic relationships and illicit affairs galore. “We made sure that when you come back to Tony, Rupert, Declan and their rivalry, it felt even more dangerous, even darker, with higher stakes and more emotion. That gives you a muscular story taking you through the show,” writer and producer Dominic Treadwell-Collins says. “I think this is a much more mature, much more confident show. We go to some dark places but always make sure there’s a light in the dark.” But there’s another reason we adore Rivals. The stunning locations featured in the first series were the talk of the Condé Nast Traveller office – sprawling Cotswolds landscapes, majestic mansions, glitzy parties all sparked interest and intrigue in the region – and the second season was no different. "I wanted to be darker and bolder with more contrasting and clashing colours within the Corinium studio sets," says Dominic Hyman, production designer. “This year we leaned into rich purples and mauves, which contrasted really nicely with the established oranges, golds and blacks of Corinium. I hope people will notice how Tony Baddingham's desperate, out-of-control ego drives the scale and ambition of the set designs at Corinium. The sets get bigger, gaudier and more and more extreme. This is the opposite of Venturer’s approach, which is about filming in the community, where people are the real subjects, not expensive and gaudy studio sets.” Here, we check in on some of the prettiest locations used in the filming of Rivals. Where was Rivals season 2 part 1 filmed? When asked about his favourite filming locations from season two of Rivals, locations manager Joel Holmes answered: "Canons House on the harbour-side in Bristol. It’s a large, vacant 1980s-style office premises that used to be home to Lloyds Insurance and is awaiting redevelopment. It was perfect for our period and served as a variety of sets for the series: a Manhattan restaurant, Heathrow Airport Arrivals, the IBA exterior, foyer and corridors, and The Scorpion’s office foyer. "We created our own polo pitch in the grounds of Berkeley Castle for the Rutshire Cup sequence in episode one, but also used Beaufort Polo Club near Tetbury in Gloucestershire for close-up ‘in-game’ elements. Beaufort also gave our cast riding lessons throughout the series. “Travelling to Ireland was a really cool experience – she [Cameron Cook] got to produce outside of the country with Declan, to create something of their own,” says Nafessa Williams, who plays Cook. "That was really exciting, and definitely one of the highlights for Cameron this season. It was my first time there, but we were there when it was very wet, very rainy and cold because it was the middle of winter. It was a challenging day, but fun too. We all laugh and joke about it. We were there for a couple of days – the second day, the weather got a lot better and the sun started to come out. The first day, we were up against a lot of wind, rain, mud, so you’ve got to shoot with urgency because you’re fighting the weather.” Rivals is set in the quaint countryside setting of Rutshire. While the village is technically fictional, much of the filming took place across the Cotswolds, where author of the original book series, Jilly Cooper, has lived for decades. The production team took over the Gloucestershire village of Tetbury for around a week of filming, replacing signs around the village and ensuring the shopfronts were transported back to the 1980s. Neston Park stands in as the home of David Tennant’s character, Lord Tony Baddingham, where the garden party scenes take place early in the series. The grand country house dates back to the late 18th century, but the estate was initially built in the 15th century. It’s a private estate and not open to the public, except for a section of the estate’s woods open for locals and customers of Neston Farm Shop. The TV studios were built at TBY2, a new production site at The Bottle Yard Studios in Bristol. The state-of-the-art studios are the largest in the West of England and offer 11 stages for filming. A handful of other scenes were filmed in and around the city, with shots in Queen Square and outside the Harbour Hotel Bristol. Nafessa Williams, who plays Cameron Cook, said on shooting in Bristol: “It’s not my first time in Bristol this go round. I know the lay of the land, I know my way around, and I’m more connected to the cast. It’s like my sophomore year – you come back, and you know where everything is. I actually started to miss Bristol after a while. When it was time to come back, I was like, I think I miss Bristol a good bit. It was easier this time – less of a transition. Bristol kind of felt like home. I had a really lovely flat on the water in the harbourside, which made it sweeter too.” The Wiltshire market town of Corsham stood in for the fictional village of Cotchester. Corsham High Street was transformed into an 1980s scene, and the historic buildings made for a perfect, quintessentially English backdrop. Where was Rivals season 2 part two filmed? The new locations revealed The wait is almost over. The second half of Rivals season 2 lands on Disney+ on 11 November, bringing us back to the scandalous world of Rutshire's wealthy elite, where lavish parties, complicated love affairs and plenty of drama are never far away. And while the fictional county remains at the heart of the action, filming has taken the cast and crew to some rather spectacular real-life locations across the UK. From historic churches and grand hotels to Bristol's bustling waterfront, here are some of the places used to bring the latest season to life. One of Bristol's most impressive landmarks, St Mary Redcliffe Church is a magnificent example of Gothic architecture, with soaring vaulted ceilings, intricate stonework and beautiful stained-glass windows. The historic church provides the setting for a funeral scene in the second half of season two, making it one of the few locations specifically confirmed for the new episodes. Located just a short walk from Bristol's harbourside, the church is open to visitors outside services and special events. Overlooking College Green in the heart of Bristol, the Bristol Marriott Royal Hotel is a grand Victorian building that has been welcoming guests since 1868. Its elegant interiors make an appearance in season two, doubling as a nightclub for a scene involving Maud and Declan O'Hara. With its ornate architecture and central location, the hotel is also a convenient base for exploring the city, with Bristol Cathedral and the harbourside just a short stroll away. Another Bristol landmark that makes an appearance in season two is the Bristol Hippodrome, one of the city's best-known theatres. Opened in 1912, the historic venue has hosted everything from West End musicals to ballet and opera over the years. For Rivals, its stage door was transformed into the entrance of a London theatre, allowing the production to recreate a West End setting without leaving Bristol. Just around the corner, Denmark Street was also used during filming for the second season. Tucked away in the city centre, the historic street is home to theatres, bars and independent businesses, and is an easy stop for fans hoping to explore some of the filming locations on foot. Bristol's waterfront also provided a backdrop for filming, with Canons Wharf among the locations used by the production. Its historic warehouses, waterside buildings and busy promenades offer a different setting from the sprawling country estates that dominate the series. Today, the harbourside is one of the city's liveliest neighbourhoods, home to restaurants, galleries and cultural attractions, including the Arnolfini contemporary arts centre and M Shed museum. A more unusual filming location is Aerospace Bristol, the aviation museum just north of the city centre. Home to the last Concorde ever built and flown, the museum was used during the first season of Rivals, with the supersonic aircraft providing a suitably glamorous backdrop for the jet-setting characters. According to local reporting, the museum also features in season two, although its appearance in the remaining episodes has not been confirmed. Visitors can step aboard Concorde Alpha Foxtrot and explore the museum's collection of aircraft and aviation exhibits.

item.title: Where to Find 15 of Philly's Best Cheesesteaks, According to a Longtime Local
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
The City of Brotherly Love is filled with meat-and-cheese sandwich lovers. Philadelphia is defined by the big three: Hoagies (loaded Italian and chicken cutlet sandwiches), roast pork (with garlicky broccoli rabe and sharp provolone), and cheesesteaks. The cheesesteak's story began in the 1930s in South Philadelphia but has become a staple at corner shops across the region, given the gourmet remix by award-winning chefs, and even inspired international outposts in Tokyo and London. I've been eating cheesesteaks since my college days, and as a Philly lifer, I've got plenty of opinions. Consider this your beginner’s guide. Cheesesteaks are as much a part of Philly's late-night food culture as they are a daytime attraction, especially on weekends and game days. Expect long lines, limited seating, and plenty of takeout orders at popular spots, and bring cash—many old-school shops don't accept cards. Like New York's pizza slice culture, cheesesteaks are typically eaten on the go or at a nearby outdoor table. Grab extra napkins and come hungry. A classic Philly cheesesteak starts with thinly sliced ribeye steak, melted cheese, and a long Italian roll. But no two shops make it exactly the same, and everyone has their preferences. The meat: Some shops finely chop their ribeye on the grill, while others leave it in thin slices or longer strips. It comes down to whether you prefer a finely chopped, cheesy mixture or more substantial bites of steak. The cheese and toppings: American, Cheez Whiz, and provolone are the traditional choices. In Philly, you'll hear people order their preferred cheese "wit" or "without," referring to fried onions. For example, "Whiz wit" means Cheez Whiz with onions, while "American without" means American cheese without onions. Other popular toppings include mushrooms, sweet or hot peppers, which you can often request on the side. The bread: A good cheesesteak roll is typically long and Italian-style, sometimes seeded, with a lightly crunchy crust and soft interior—similar to New Orleans French bread. Some shops scoop out the excess bread to make more room for the steak and cheese, while others leave the roll intact. Either way, the bread needs to hold up to all that juicy filling. Where to find Philly cheesesteaks by neighborhood and style 14 E. Snyder Ave. Philadelphia, PA 19148 John’s on East Snyder Avenue has been a neighborhood fixture for nearly a century, thanks to the Bucci family. The James Beard Award-winning shop has also been voted Best Cheesesteak multiple times, known for its hefty portions of finely chopped, crispy ribeye steak served on crusty rolls sourced from nearby Carangi’s or Sarcone’s. Choose from American, provolone, or Cooper Sharp cheese. Expect long lines, but there’s outdoor seating and a semi-enclosed dining area where you can dig in. And if you’ve got the appetite, don’t leave without trying their signature roast pork sandwich. You’ve probably heard the hype or seen the long lines on 9th Street. Every cheesesteak at Angelo’s is made with house-baked, crusty bread and fresh, peppery ribeye steak, with your choice of Cooper Sharp or the increasingly popular long-hot-pepper-infused Cheez Whiz. Since its Italian Market debut, the Michelin Bib Gourmand-recognized shop has expanded beyond its Italian Street location, including an outpost at a food hall in Wilmington, Delaware and a ghost kitchen deeper in South Philly, with more locations on the horizon. Philadelphia is lucky to have two Jim’s Steaks, each with its own personality. The 50-year-old Jim’s South Street is where all walks of life congregate late into the night, plotting their orders (definitely get the famous Whiz wit), scrambling for cash (there’s an ATM inside that sometimes works), and hollering at motorbikes cruising by. Inside, there’s a first-floor diner-style dining room and a second floor adorned with rare mosaics by the late legendary Philadelphia artist Isaiah Zagar, whose Philadelphia’s Magic Gardens is just a few blocks west. Over in West Philly, Jim’s West—the original location, now under different ownership—sits on a residential corner where O.G.s line up to bring cheesesteaks home to family and friends or score a $20 combo special: a beef or chicken cheesesteak, a drink, and a side of banana pudding. Recently featured in season six of Abbott Elementary, the nearly 50-year-old Ishkabibble’s has long attracted celebrities, locals, and tourists alike, often captured on camera by local photographer South Street Sam. The shop helped popularize chicken cheesesteaks and hot pepper-and-onion Spanish fries, eventually expanding to a second, larger location with additional seating just two blocks away. Chicken cheesesteaks are the name of the game here, with nearly a dozen variations, including Pizza (mozzarella and pizza sauce), South Philly (roasted peppers, spinach, and provolone), and Broccoli (melted cheese and steamed broccoli). Wash it all down with their famous Gremlin, a half-grape soda, half-lemonade concoction. Trust us. What began as a Northeast Philly corner shop in 1949 has changed owners, locations, and names over the decades, but one thing remains: its signature thinly sliced ribeye cheesesteaks, grilled to order with or without onions on fresh Liscio's rolls delivered daily. In 2013, the renamed shop landed at Fishtown's buzzy corner of Girard and Frankford avenues, transforming into a family-friendly, '50s-style diner with an expanded menu. Alongside its classic cheesesteaks, you'll find vegetarian versions with onions and mushrooms, gluten-free roll options, crinkle-cut fries, egg creams, and sundaes. 1338 S. 10th Street Philadelphia, PA 19147 Got cheesesteak FOMO because you're vegan? Or have plant-based loved ones who want in on the Philly experience? Triangle Tavern, a neighborhood bar on East Passyunk Avenue, has you covered. Most of the menu is vegetarian or vegan, including its only cheesesteak, which was crowned Best Vegan Cheesesteak in Philly by the American Vegan Center in 2019. The winning sandwich features locally owned Blackbird Foods' seitan, fried onions, and a Carangi Bakery roll, all smothered in house-made vegan Whiz (a blend of Daiya vegan cheddar, Tofutti cream cheese, miso, nutritional yeast, and seasonings). For decades, Robert Perry has cultivated a community of artists, musicians, creatives, and beer lovers at this two-story rock-and-roll bar known for its sticker- and graffiti-covered walls. Affectionately called TMoms by locals, Tattooed Mom welcomes meat lovers and plant-based eaters alike with a savory, gooey vegan cheesesteak. Chunks of seitan and plant-based smoked Gouda replace the traditional steak and Whiz, all tucked into a crusty roll from local bakery Merzbacher's of Germantown. Even better, you can snag one for just $7 on Meatless Mondays. 4540 Baltimore Ave. Philadelphia, PA 19143 A West Philly institution, this husband-and-wife-run Ethiopian restaurant and bar is known for its mashup of East African and Philly staples, particularly its berbere-spiced beef cheesesteaks, served since 1996. Thinly sliced beef is coated in an earthy, fiery blend of chili peppers, coriander, ginger, cardamom, nutmeg, and allspice, then tossed with onions and melted American cheese. The result is a juicy, boldly seasoned cheesesteak with a kick. 1600 W. Girard Ave. Philadelphia, PA 19130 Fairmount may not be the first neighborhood that comes to mind for a Philly cheesesteak, but it's home to an 8,500-square-foot indoor mini golf course serving pan-Asian-inspired bar food. Opened in 2021 by three longtime friends, Libertee Grounds has a playful menu to match, including an Indian-inspired Lamb Kheema cheesesteak made with a masala-rubbed lamb and ribeye blend, melted Cooper Sharp, caramelized onions, and cilantro-lime aioli on a seeded long roll. It comes with fries, but for an extra kick, add pickled Fresno peppers or miso Cooper Sharp cheese Whiz. 3401 Walnut St. Franklin's Table Food Hall, Philadelphia, PA 19104 2563 Trenton Ave. Philadelphia, PA 19125 What began as a food cart in 2022 has grown into multiple Philadelphia locations for Korea Taqueria, where chef-owners Alexander Sherack and Rene Lopez blend traditional Korean flavors with Mexican street food staples. Their Korean-Mexican mashups include a signature slow-burn spicy bulgogi cheesesteak featuring thinly sliced halal ribeye marinated in bulgogi sauce, melted Cooper Sharp, gochujang mayo, and scallions on a seeded Liscio's hoagie roll. Add cucumber kimchi for an extra tangy crunch. Husband-and-wife team Steve and Margie Kotridis have kept this Northwest Philly cheesesteak shop humming with hungry customers since taking over in 2008. Now one of three Michelin Bib Gourmand-recognized cheesesteak shops in Philadelphia, alongside Del Rossi's and Angelo's, Dalessandro's is known for its juicy, gooey, squishy sandwiches. Finely minced ribeye, melted cheese, and generously diced onions meld together inside Amoroso's hearth-baked rolls (another local favorite bakery), which soak up all that goodness. Better yet, toppings are free. Grab your cheesesteak to go and, weather permitting, enjoy it beneath the trees at the park across the street. 3653 Germantown Ave.Philadelphia, PA 19140 This North Philly cheesesteak shop is a celebrity in its own right, having appeared in Creed and Creed II and attracted famous fans like Philly's own Colman Domingo. Since 1994, crowds have lined up beneath its glowing red neon sign near the Broad and Erie transit hub for finely chopped "100% sirloin steak," served in half, whole (12-inch), or Giant (two-foot) portions. Order yours Whiz wit (ketchup is a popular addition here), grab some cheese fries, and join the regulars eating off the hoods of their cars. Those in the know head next door to Eagle Bar for a beer before calling it a night. 3020 S. Broad St. Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19145 Heading down to the stadiums for a game? Consider Skinny Joey's your pre- or post-game cheesesteak fix. Former inmate turned podcaster turned restaurateur Joey Merlino has entered Philly's competitive cheesesteak scene, offering six beef and chicken variations that draw long lines of customers and parked cars along Broad Street on weekends. And he's not stopping there: Merlino has expanded to the Jersey Shore with a Wildwood outpost. Competition and tradition run deep in Philly's cheesesteak scene, a challenge Nish Patel embraced when he took over Del Rossi's in 2020. He helped usher in a new wave of cheesesteak making by focusing on better ingredients and technique rather than reinventing the classic sandwich. First came a house-baked roll with a crunchy crust and pillowy-soft interior. Next, pasture-raised, hormone-free, hand-cut ribeye steak, followed by melted Cooper Sharp American cheese and onions. The upgrades paid off: Del Rossi's earned Michelin Bib Gourmand recognition in 2026. One of Philly's newest cheesesteak sensations, Sal Burgese's Backyard Cravings began as pandemic-era home cooking for friends, family, and a few lucky guests at his South Philly rowhome. What started in his backyard grew into tailgating parties and, eventually, his first brick-and-mortar shop in October 2026. Like Del Rossi's, the focus here is on quality ingredients and cooking from scratch. The $20+ cheesesteak has a generous portion of finely chopped, salt-and-pepper-seasoned beef, onions, and creamy Cooper Sharp cheese on a long, crisp, sesame-seeded roll with a soft, scooped-out center. Burgese's cheesesteaks have drawn sold-out crowds wherever he's served them, so for now, the Eagles “Kelly Green” and cream-colored corner spot sells them only on weekends.

item.title: IDEA: Walk the talk: a week learning French with a personal prof in Normandy
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
I’m walking beside the River Seine in the French city of Rouen when I realise that I’ve been speaking French – without pausing to find a word or struggle with grammar – for five whole minutes. Anna, my French “prof” for the week, nods encouragingly and so I continue. It’s a breakthrough moment, if only for my confidence. This is the last day of a DIY language course that I devised when Rouen’s language schools told me they were full for the only week I could get away. When I then enquired about their private tutors, I was told no one was available. This turned out to save me a pretty penny: language school tutors cost €60 an hour while Anna – who I discovered on the website Apprentus – is a cost-effective €19 an hour. For the last couple of winters I’ve tried to spend a week or so brushing up my “intermediate” French language skills, in situ. A spate of new research on the remarkable cognitive benefits of learning a second language have made me a keen user of apps and podcasts – and yet no amount of AI-generated tutoring can compete with talking to (and being corrected and helped by) a real person. Learning in situ also comes with a chance to travel, to communicate with dozens of people, to experience the culture that accompanies the language one is trying so hard to learn. Last winter, I went to a language school in Montpellier. Three hours a day didn’t come cheap. The class was large: 12 pupils from across the world. I spent my mornings pinned to a plastic chair in a cramped, tatty classroom, listening to my peers struggle through various exercises. This isn’t the best way to learn. A recent study published in Nature suggests that moving helps us concentrate, remember and generally learn more effectively. Little wonder that I left Montpellier feeling I hadn’t learned much. So I was delighted when Anna suggested that we do our two-hour classes on foot round Rouen. “If it rains,” she said, “we can talk over goûter.” Le Goûter is the French tradition of taking a small snack between lunch and dinner – a bit like English teatime. Having booked Anna (a political sciences student at the University of Rouen Normandy) for 10 hours of French conversation over five days, I reserved a studio apartment (bang in the historic heart of Rouen for less than £60 a night) and bought a ferry ticket from Newhaven to Dieppe. Rouen is a one-hour train journey from the port, and the combined ferry-train ticket (return) cost a thrifty £65. Anna and I met outside the ornate Saint-Maclou church, clearly both a little nervous. After all, we were about to spend 10 hours alone together, with no prior knowledge of each other. It also turned out that I was Anna’s first pupil since she’d registered on Apprentus. Moreover, she had signed up expecting to help kids with their homework. Instead she got me – a woman old enough to be her mother. We needn’t have worried. Anna had come straight from a (peaceful) protest march, and within minutes we were chatting away about the concerns of French students, as we strolled. Anna doubled as a tour guide, showing me all her favourite corners of Rouen – while simultaneously correcting my French. When it rained, she introduced me to Rouen’s best tea houses (the Dame Cakes salon de thé was a particular favourite), in effect doubling as my dining companion. While Anna’s first language is French, she also speaks excellent English, meaning she could explain complex grammar to me. Her Senegal heritage meant that I also learned about the turbulent history of west Africa, as well as being brought up to speed on the ongoing student protests. We spent one fascinating lesson – which also involved riding Rouen’s buses – discussing Senegal’s matrilineal history of priestesses and queens, in French. Who knew? Not me! Anna’s suggestions for lessons included an outing to Rouen’s Musée des Beaux-Arts (free, as are most of Rouen’s museums) which bills itself as France’s biggest impressionist collection outside Paris. We walked Rouen’s riverside pathways, which run for miles up and down the Seine, and ambled through the city’s beautiful, medieval quarters, stopping to explore areas such as the Place du Vieux-Marché, where Joan of Arc was burned alive. As these areas are largely car-free, we didn’t have to worry about dodging mopeds or shouting over the roar of traffic. I could have hired Anna for longer, but two hours of one-to-one tuition each day felt optimal for my brain as it struggled to recall a very distant French A-level. I used the rest of my time to read a French novel, listen to French radio and TV, and wander Rouen with the self-challenge of talking to as many people as I could. Imagine my delight when, on my last day, a shop assistant asked me if I was local! Anna and I finished our week with hugs and promises to keep in touch. My “prof” (the French abbreviation of professeur/e, commonly used to mean teacher) had proved to be informative, knowledgable, cost effective and great fun. And my six days, including food, transport, tutor and accommodation, had cost little more than £600. On the ferry home, I couldn’t help wondering if human connections like this – an on-foot tutor, guide and new best friend rolled into one – might be the (fun) future of language learning. Annabel Abbs (writing as Annabel Streets) is the author of The Walking Cure, published by Bloomsbury (£10.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. item.title: REVIEW: 9 All-Inclusive Resorts in Cancún That Go Way Beyond an Open Bar
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
I first arrived in Cancún, Mexico, more than 20 years ago. I had big hair, pencil-thin eyebrows, and limited expectations for an all-inclusive vacation: A swim-up bar serving frozen margaritas was about all I needed. Since then, my priorities have shifted, and thankfully, Cancún’s all-inclusive resorts have grown up alongside me. After two decades of return visits made easier by an abundance of nonstop US flights, I’ve become more discerning about what deserves a place in that up-front price. I’ve also discovered that Cancún’s enduring spring break reputation tells an incomplete story about what's on offer. Choose the right resort, and you can have a butler draw your evening bath, a private pool overlooking the Caribbean, and à la carte restaurants you’ll look forward to all afternoon, whether you prefer the Hotel Zone’s long sweep of white sand, the relative quiet of Playa Mujeres, or a boat ride out to Isla Mujeres. The frozen margaritas are still here. But now, there’s much more worth checking in for. Read on for the best all-inclusive resorts in Cancún worth planning a vacation around. FAQ: What is the best all-inclusive resort in Cancún? For an adult-only stay, Le Blanc Spa Resort Cancún gets my vote. Butler service and French tasting menus make it feel suitably indulgent, and the rate includes access to the spa’s hydrotherapy circuit. With children, I’d choose Finest Playa Mujeres, where separate kids' bedrooms and supervised care during mealtimes give parents a holiday too. Is it worth getting an all-inclusive package in Cancún? Yes, especially if you plan to spend most of your vacation at the resort. At the right property, your rate covers dinners you actually look forward to, premium drinks, and activities you’d otherwise pay for separately. If you plan to spend each day exploring and eating around town, a traditional hotel may make more sense. Before booking your all-inclusive, be sure to check the exclusions—you might find you'll have to pay extra for spa treatments, special bottles of wine, and some restaurant experiences. What’s the cheapest month to go to Cancún? September is generally one of the cheapest months for Cancún hotels, after summer vacation crowds leave. The trade-off is wetter weather and the possibility of tropical storms during hurricane season. For a better balance of price and weather, consider late October through the week before Thanksgiving. How we choose the best all-inclusive resorts in Cancún Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

item.title: Author Jojo Moyes among UK travellers at risk of EU ban amid digital border system glitches
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
The writer Jojo Moyes is facing a two-year EU travel ban and €10,000 (£8,300) fine because of glitches with the bloc’s digital security controls. She is one of a number of UK travellers who say their trips to the EU have not been properly recorded since the introduction of the EU digital entry and exit system (EES). The system, which launched last year, has replaced passport stamps with biometrics recorded at border control in Schengen zone countries. However, the botched rollout has led to some Britons being denied their post-Brexit right to spend 90 days out of 180 in Europe because the system falsely states they have used up their allowance. Moyes, a bestselling novelist, was detained by French border guards after a holiday and accused of overstaying. She had spent only 23 days in the EU over six months. She discovered that her departure from Portugal after a trip in May had not been logged on the system. “The clock had been ticking ever since,” she told the consumer organisation Which? “The border control senior officer at Marseille warned me that I should not attempt to re-enter Europe until it is sorted out, or face a €10,000 fine and a two-year ban.” The problem affects passengers whose biometrics were collected on their arrival in the EU, but not on their departure. In some cases, this means the system has failed to record that they have left. The rolling 180-day window starts as soon as they enter the EU and, since Brexit, those who are deemed to have remained for more than 90 days face deportation or fines of up to €10,000. Jane Nolan and her husband discovered that the EES wrongly showed them as having used up their 90-day travel allowance, preventing them from booking a trip to France. “We travelled to France in April by LeShuttle and spent 40 days there,” she said. “We have made no subsequent Schengen visits. “We should have 50 days remaining, but the EU’s ‘check how long you can stay’ tool says: ‘Authorised stay: not OK,’ and zero remaining days. It does not show us which entry or exit record produced that result.” The couple’s passports were manually stamped on their return to the UK in June as French authorities had suspended the EES to prevent long queues. “We have asked the French authorities to check our records, but do not yet know what has gone wrong or whether the result could affect us at the border,” said Nolan. In a case reported by the Telegraph a holidaymaker from the UK was detained at the Italian border and deported under police guard after a system error suggested she had overstayed in the EU. Rory Boland, Editor of Which? Travel described the situation as unacceptable. “This is one of the most serious in a long line of European border control failures,” he said. “The lack of care and accountability shown towards travellers, who risk being locked up and fines of thousands of pounds for rules they have not broken, is utterly indefensible.” The Advantage Travel Partnership, which represents independent travel agents, said British travellers were being penalised for a chaotic system. Its CEO, Julia Lo Bue-Said, said: “Travellers should not be penalised for failures in a system that is entirely outside their control. There needs to be greater accountability, alongside a straightforward process to challenge and correct inaccurate records.” The Foreign Office said the problem was concerning. A spokesperson said: “We are aware of reports of inaccuracies in some EES records affecting British nationals, including incomplete records and the registration of some individuals who are exempt from EES. We are raising these issues as part of our engagement with the European Commission.” It advised travellers to carry evidence of when they last left the EU and to raise any anomalies with border officials. Travellers can check how many days of their allowance they have left by typing their passport number into the EES website. This records all visits to the Schengen zone since 10 April 2026. If there is an unexpected shortfall, they can ask to have their record corrected before travelling by selecting the last country they visited on the Travel to Europe data protection page and contacting the relevant data controller. Moyes said her efforts to do this have so far been in vain. “In the last two weeks, I’ve tried every possible avenue,” she said. “I have now engaged an immigration lawyer, but not everyone is lucky enough to be able to afford this remedy. I have no idea how much time they think I have spent in Europe, and no idea whether I am safe to travel.” The European Commission has been contacted for a comment.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: How to Spend a Rainy Day in New York City
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
A rainy day in New York City is no new phenomenon, but that doesn’t make its occurrence any less disappointing. According to reporting from News 12, Central Park only reported nine completely dry weekends out of the past 40 weekends of 2026, putting a real—forgive me—damper on park hangs and beach days. In case you count yourself among the masses with foiled plans, we at Condé Nast Traveler have you covered. Our editors have weathered their fair share of cold and dreary days in the city and learned to love the rain. After all, it’s the best excuse to dry off by the crackling fireplace of a plush hotel lobby, or conversely, to take a dip into the steaming Russian Turkish baths to cure the sinking cold. Instead of willing the clouds to part, bear your galoshes and head to our editors’ favorite things to do in New York City on a rainy day. That travel editors love a hotel lobby is about as unsurprising as a dad joke, but there’s nothing like a mini staycation to salvage a lost weekend. Commerce writer Jessica Chapel is partial to The Hotel Chelsea. The neighborhood institution has moved far past its roach-ridden days when Patti Smith and Robert Mapplethorpe were Just Kids, and the experience of their lobby is the apotheosis of that evolution. There’s a lot of modern polish, sure, but all the charming verdigris has been kept intact. There’s the art from the hotel’s most (in)famous guests splashed over the walls, the wrought iron chandeliers bathing the space in romantic lighting, and the aforementioned fireplace tying a bow around the mood. Plus, it doesn’t hurt that the hotel’s Lobby Bar is just right next door. If Chelsea feels like a slog to commute to, there are plenty of great options scattered across the map, from the Ace Hotel Brooklyn which has plenty of public workspaces, or Times Square’s Algonquin Hotel, which saw the genesis of The New Yorker just 100 years ago. Get lost inside a small museum or gallery The easiest remedy for rainy day restlessness is to stretch your legs at one of the city’s finest museums, though even the impressive 2.2 million-square-foot expanse of the Met becomes easily dwarfed when you’re crammed in by a surge of fellow museum-goers who had the exact same idea. Instead, spend your day exploring NYC’s smaller scholarly corners. Editorial assistant Skyli Alvarez heads to East Williamsburg art organization Amant whenever she feels like she’s cooped inside her apartment, watching the hours just slip away. To start, there’s no need to worry about ponying up big ticket prices as entry is always free. “Peruse the titles at Kis Café and Bookstore, then head to gallery spaces 932 Grand and 315 Maujer; across the street, you’ll find multimedia installations in Géza,” says Alvarez, “The exhibit Sentient Earth currently spans all three galleries, bringing together 28 artists to examine the ways we’ve impacted the planet (and what—if it gained sentience—its response to us might be). Do explore Amant's event programming of screenings and panels, which you can find here.” Other small but mighty options include the Financial District’s public poetry library Poets House, which overlooks the Hudson and Bushwick’s Bone Museum, which also houses resident tuxedo cat Bone Jovi. Explore New York's finest movie theaters Film critic Anthony Lane once posited, “as a rough rule, cinema can be sundered into two halves: six-o’clock films and nine-o’clock films,” and a rainy day is certainly the occasion for the six-o’clock variety and all its ritual: rallying a group to go with, booking the early dinner reservation, whiling away at a nearby bar after to unpack what you’ve just seen. Commerce director Madison Flager likes the Lincoln Center AMC, home to the largest IMAX screen in the country, clocking in at 75.6 feet tall by 101 feet wide, which is roughly the size of a 10-story building. News editor Hannah Towey, on the other hand, dodges the rain at the Metrograph, a boutique two-screen theater keeping the spirit of Prohibition-era New York alive and well. Whichever way you lean, you can always count on NYC’s trusty movie theaters to show you something new. The less-than-stellar weather shouldn’t keep you from embarking on a treasure hunt, and doing your due diligence enclosed inside one of the city’s coolest vintage stores is a surefire way to uncover a few gems. Alvarez recommends the Flatiron District’s Surrender Dorothy, where the racks are piled with the well-loved and pristine, collector’s items and forgotten blasts from the past, avant-garde art pieces, and buy-it-for-life workwear. It’s dopamine dressing at its best. You could also try your luck at one of the city’s larger franchises like Beacon’s Closet, or, if you’re willing to face the elements, dive into a flea market. One of the best spots to people-watch in the city, come rain or shine, is the baths. And having a place to hide from the chill and unforgiving precipitation is a welcome bonus. Commerce writer Jessica Sulima touts the East Village’s Russian Turkish Baths as the perfect place to drop by. Melt away whatever’s ailing you in the 215 °F Russian Sauna, and if you need any help doing so, get the platza oak leaf ritual where spa employees forcefully smack your pores open with bushels of oak leaves in the sauna. If you’re looking for something a little more communal, Flager likes to warm up at Othership, which sets itself apart with its guided wellness experiences that combine breath work, aromatherapy, visualizations, somatic movement, live music, and group “shares.” Nothing brings a bar together like its pool table, but if you’ve spent more time watching the queue of quarters waiting for your turn than the game itself, head to a dedicated pool hall instead, where there’s a better chance of scoring a table all your own and watching the real pros practice their hand. Union Square’s Amsterdam Billiards has been a staple ever since I came to the city five years ago. The 11,000-square-foot hall decked with its array of Brunswick tables might seem intimidating at first, but take it from a real amateur: they may be serious about their snooker here, but they’re not snobby. Pool aside, patrons keep occupied with the hall’s other offerings like table tennis, beer pong, and darts. If you’re serious about upping your game, you can even book one-hour lessons with their in-house pros. Jazz is one of the country’s greatest art forms, and New York is the genre’s most inspiring muse and resourceful studio. The city cemented its status in the 1920s Harlem Renaissance when legendary venues like the Cotton Club and Small’s Paradise put Duke Ellington, Fats Waller, and Billie Holiday in the national consciousness. Jazz in the city has traveled beyond its uptown crucible, and there’s great clubs peppered throughout the boroughs. Some of our favorites include Ornithology Jazz Club, which also has a killer vegan menu; Funny Bar, which comes from the same team as Baby’s All Right; and Greenwich Village’s Smalls Jazz Club, which keeps things true to form and no-frills. Book that tasting menu you've been putting off It’s rare in this insomniac city that you find the time for a proper, sit-down meal, let alone one that seeks to take you on a narrative journey. On a calendar-clearing day, our editors love to trawl through our map pins and notes apps for the best in slow dining. Take French-Korean bakery Lysée, famed for their trompe d'oeil pastries like the corn cake made from corn mousse, sable cookie, and grilled corn cream. Dessert is a thing of wonder here, and every Thursday night, they host “The Journey,” a tasting menu of their almost too pretty to eat creations. Tasting menus also don’t have to break the bank. Some of our top picks come in at under $150. New York’s historic theatre scene is far from confined to Broadway’s flashing lights. Some of the most exciting, intimate, and interactive productions in the city are playing Off-Broadway. Big names like Andrew Lloyd Webber have found a second wind in shows like Masquerade, a roving retelling of Phantom of the Opera, and fresh concepts like Heated Rivalry: The Unauthorized Musical Parody are attracting their own audiences with their lower budget, DIY charm. Shows like these are a trove of talent, and odds are you can find one where you won’t have to pay an arm and a leg for entry at venues like La MaMa or Signature Theatre. Associate social media manager Bridget Knowles swears by the people's princess of a dive bar as a haven from the harsh weather: “Interjecting here with what I’m sure we’re all thinking. I mean, sheesh. This is unspoken. A great dive bar is an oasis in New York City on a rainy day: a grunge mecca, a throw-some-hours-away swan song. My kind of place. A healthy dose of grime on an already lyrically imposing, moody day is great for the soul. Even if you’re off the Miller High Life (ah, it hurt to type, but pun intended) one of the greatest pastimes in life, according to me, is to simply load up touch tunes and shoot at a table a bit. Make some friends, watch something insane playing on a corner TV. You know, commiserate. Get your hands on some of the best in the city here.”
